note: Neon's answers. Edit this file to change what Neon says: each entry has the question, other ways of asking it, keywords, the answer, links and related questions.

entries.q: What is Kawkit?
entries.a:
Kawkit tells you how to split a marketing budget across channels, and how sure it is.

You upload weekly spend and revenue. It works out how much revenue each channel brought in, then recommends a split, with every number shown as a range instead of a single figure.

No code is needed, and you can explore a finished example without an account.

entries.q: What is marketing mix modelling?
alt: what is a media mix model
how does mmm work in simple terms
entries.a:
Marketing mix modelling (MMM) explains your sales over time from everything that could have driven them: what you spent on each channel, the season, promotions, and events like Black Friday.

It looks at weeks when you spent more or less on a channel and asks what happened to sales, after allowing for everything else. From that it estimates what each channel is worth.

It needs no cookies or user tracking, only weekly totals.

entries.q: Who is Kawkit for?
alt: do i need to be a data scientist
i am not technical can i use it
entries.a:
It is built for a marketing or growth manager who owns a budget across about 3 to 10 channels and can export weekly numbers to a spreadsheet. You do not need to code or know statistics.

Analysts get more out of it too: you can add what you know from experiments, check convergence, and download the detail.

entries.q: How do I get started?
alt: how to run my first model
entries.a:
1. Open the sample result to see what you will get.
2. Use "Check my data" to see if your own file is ready. It runs in your browser and nothing is sent anywhere.
3. Sign in, load your data, optionally add what you already know, and submit.
4. The model fits in the background, usually in a few minutes. Then read the "In short" box at the top of the result.

entries.q: Is Kawkit free?
entries.a: Yes. The sample results, the data check and running your own models are all free. There are fair-use limits: one model running and two waiting at a time, and 20 submissions a day.

entries.q: Do I need an account?
alt: can i use it without signing up
can i try without an account
entries.a:
Not to look around. Without an account you can explore the sample results, read the lessons page, and check whether your own data is ready.

You need an account to fit a model on your data, because the file has to be stored and the run takes a few minutes. Signing up takes an email and a password.

entries.q: How is this different from last-click attribution or Google Analytics?
alt: why not just use google analytics
difference between mmm and multi touch attribution
why do results differ from ga
entries.a:
Last-click reports give all the credit to the final thing a customer clicked. That flatters search and retargeting, and misses channels that work slowly or are never clicked, such as TV, video and outdoor.

MMM does not follow individuals at all. It compares weeks: when spend on a channel went up or down, did sales follow, after allowing for season and events? That lets it value every channel on the same footing, including offline ones, and it keeps working without cookies.

The two answer different questions, so expect the numbers to differ.

entries.q: What does Bayesian mean here?
entries.a:
A Bayesian model starts from a belief about each quantity (the prior), updates it with your data, and returns the whole range of values that remain plausible (the posterior).

That gives two things an ordinary regression does not. You can feed in what you already know, such as a lift-test result. And uncertainty is measured directly, so every answer comes with an honest range and a probability.

entries.q: Why does everything come as a range instead of one number?
alt: why not just give me one number
can i get a single roi figure
entries.a:
Because a single number hides how sure anyone can be. A return of 2.0 that could really be anywhere from 0.5 to 4 should not be treated like one that is between 1.9 and 2.1.

The middle of each range (the median) is the best single guess if you need one. The width tells you how much to trust it. Wide ranges are a finding, not a fault: they tell you where an experiment would pay off.

entries.q: What is the sample result?
alt: tell me about the sample data
where does the example data come from
entries.a:
There are six finished results to explore, no account needed.

One uses made-up data where the true answers are known, so you can see the model recover them. Five use real, anonymised e-commerce brands (home decor, skincare, apparel, food and drink, dental care) from a public dataset. The real ones are messier and each page says plainly how far to trust it.

entries.q: What did fitting real brands teach the model?
alt: what went wrong on real data
entries.a:
Fitting five real brands changed the model in six ways. The first real fit credited advertising with 122% of revenue, which is impossible, so the baseline can no longer go negative. The starting assumptions turned out to imply absurd returns and were recalibrated. Calendar events and one economic measure cut errors a lot; weather did not help at all.

The lessons page records what broke, what changed, and what was tried and thrown away.

entries.q: What data do I need?
alt: what do i need to upload
what inputs does the model need
entries.a:
One spreadsheet with one row per week, containing:

- a date
- revenue (or whatever you want to explain: sales, orders, sign-ups)
- what you spent on each channel that week, one column per channel
- optionally, other things that move sales, such as a promotion flag or price

At least 52 weeks are needed, and two years or more gives steadier results. Your column names do not have to match a template; you can say which column is which after loading.

entries.q: What file format and column names does it expect?
alt: how should i name the columns
entries.a:
It reads CSV files. The built-in layout is:

- date, as YYYY-MM-DD
- revenue
- spend_<channel> for each channel, for example spend_tv
- control_<name> for anything else, for example control_promo

You do not have to use it. If your columns have other names, a screen appears where you pick what each one is, and common date formats are converted for you. From Excel or Google Sheets, export as CSV, or paste a Google Sheets link.

entries.q: How much history do I need?
alt: can i use 6 months of data
entries.a:
At least 52 weeks, or the model will not run. 104 weeks or more is recommended.

With under 78 weeks the model cannot learn a yearly seasonal pattern, because it has not seen a full cycle twice. More history also means more ups and downs in spend to learn from, which narrows the ranges.

entries.q: Can I upload daily data?
entries.a:
Yes. Daily rows are added up into weeks starting on Monday, and incomplete weeks at either end are left out. The model itself always works on weeks.

Monthly data is not supported: there would be too few points, and carry-over between weeks could not be seen. Rows must be either 7 days or 1 day apart.

entries.q: What are the size limits for a file?
alt: how many channels can i have
entries.a:
A file can have up to 15 spend channels, 5,000 rows and 10 MB, and needs at least 52 weekly rows.

If you have more than 15 channels, combine small or similar ones, for example all display networks into one. Many small channels are hard to tell apart anyway.

entries.q: My columns have different names. What do I do?
alt: how does the column mapper work
my file does not match the template
entries.a:
Nothing in advance. Load the file and a screen called "Tell us which column is which" appears, with a first guess for every column: date, revenue, advertising spend, outside factor, or leave out.

Change anything that is wrong, give each channel a short name, pick how your dates are written, and choose "Use these columns".

entries.q: Which date formats are accepted?
alt: what date formats can i use
entries.a:
Through the column mapper: 2024-03-25, 25/03/2024, 03/25/2024, 2024/03/25, and written dates such as 25 Mar 2024.

If every date could be read as either day-first or month-first, it assumes day first and tells you, so you can switch it. A file that already uses the template must have dates as YYYY-MM-DD.

entries.q: Can I model something other than revenue?
alt: can i use orders or sign ups
entries.a:
Yes. Put any one number per week in the revenue column: sales, orders, sign-ups, leads or profit.

Bear in mind that "ROI" then means that number per unit of spend. For orders, an ROI of 0.02 means 2 orders per 100 spent, so "above 1" stops being the break-even line. Only one outcome can be modelled per run.

entries.q: Should I use spend, impressions or clicks for each channel?
alt: can i use impressions instead of spend
what if i only have impressions
entries.a:
Use spend. The tool reports return per unit spent and recommends a budget, and both need money as the input.

Impressions or GRPs can track exposure more closely when prices change a lot, but then "ROI" would mean revenue per impression and the budget advice would be in impressions. If you only have impressions, convert them to an approximate spend using your average cost first.

entries.q: How do I include channels I don't pay for, like email or organic social?
entries.a:
Do not add them as spend channels unless there is a real cost you could raise or lower. A spend of zero gives the model nothing to learn from.

If the activity varies and matters, add it as an outside factor instead, for example the number of emails sent that week. It then sits in the baseline, so paid channels are not credited with its sales.

entries.q: How should I group my channels?
alt: should i split facebook and instagram
entries.a:
Group by how the money works, not by how the platform reports it. A good channel is one you would actually move budget into or out of, with at least a few percent of total spend and real week-to-week variation.

Useful splits: brand search apart from generic search, and prospecting apart from retargeting, because they behave very differently. Poor splits: many tiny campaigns, or two channels that always rise and fall together, which the model cannot tell apart.

entries.q: What does 'a lot of channels for this many weeks' mean?
alt: how many channels can the model handle
entries.a:
Each channel and outside factor is something the model has to estimate. As a rule of thumb it wants about 10 weeks of data for each one. Below that it still runs, but the ranges get wide.

To fix it, add more history, or combine small and similar channels.

entries.q: What does 'spend barely changes' mean?
alt: i spend the same every week
entries.a:
The model learns a channel's effect from weeks when its spend was different. If you spend almost the same every week, there is nothing to compare, so the result for that channel will mostly repeat the starting assumption.

The fix is outside the model: vary the spend on purpose for a few weeks, or run a test, then enter what you find as a prior.

entries.q: What does 'spend mostly follows the season or trend' mean?
entries.a:
If you always spend more on a channel in the same weeks that sales are high anyway, such as the run-up to Christmas, the model cannot tell whether the ads or the season caused the sales.

The result for that channel will be uncertain and may be too generous. Adding event flags helps, and deliberately spending against the pattern for a while helps more.

entries.q: What does 'active in only a few weeks' mean?
alt: channel only ran for a short time
entries.a: The channel has spend in under 15% of your weeks. That is too little for a firm estimate, so its range will be wide. It is still worth including if the spend was large, because leaving it out would hand its sales to something else.

entries.q: What if weeks are missing from my data?
alt: i have a hole in my data
entries.a: The file is accepted with a warning, and the model treats the rows as consecutive weeks. A gap of a week or two does little harm. A long gap breaks carry-over and seasonality around it, so it is better to fill it, even with zeros for spend if you truly spent nothing.

entries.q: How should I handle unusual weeks or one-off spikes?
alt: one week had a huge spike
entries.a:
Do not delete the week. Explain it. Add an outside-factor column that is 1 in that week and 0 elsewhere, for example for a stock-out, a site outage, a product launch or a big PR moment.

The model then puts the spike in the baseline. Without it, the spike is credited to whichever channel happened to be spending most that week. On the real example brands, a few weeks drove a third to two thirds of all the error.

entries.q: How do I account for promotions, discounts or price changes?
entries.a:
Add them as outside factors. Two good ways:

- a flag: 1 in weeks a promotion ran, 0 otherwise
- a measure: your average discount percentage, or your average price, each week

Without this the model sees sales rise in promotion weeks and gives the credit to advertising.

entries.q: Should I model all revenue or only new customers?
entries.a:
It depends on the decision. If your advertising is mainly for acquisition, modelling new-customer revenue gives a cleaner read on it, because repeat purchases are driven more by email, loyalty and habit.

If you care about total sales, model all revenue, and expect a larger baseline. Do not mix the two in one run; run them separately and compare.

entries.q: Can I model several countries or products together?
entries.a:
Not in one run. Each run models one market and one outcome. For several countries or product lines, run each separately and use Compare to put two side by side.

Adding them into one file is fine only if they share the same advertising and behave alike. Otherwise the result is an average that fits none of them.

entries.q: Does currency matter?
alt: do spend and revenue need the same currency
entries.a:
Use the same currency for spend and revenue, because ROI is one divided by the other. Which currency does not matter.

Currency symbols and thousands separators in the file are stripped automatically, so "£1,234" is read as 1234.

entries.q: Is my data private? Where is it stored?
alt: who else can see the file i upload
entries.a:
Only you can read your data. That is enforced in the database itself, not only in the app.

Until you submit, your file stays in your browser. When you submit, it is stored in private storage so the model server can fit it. Results can be seen by others only if you create a share link, which you can switch off at any time.

entries.q: How long is my data kept?
alt: why did my old run disappear
entries.a:
Your 5 most recent finished runs are kept. When a 6th finishes, the oldest run and its file are deleted at once, and you are warned before submitting.

Failed and cancelled runs are deleted after 7 days. Accounts with no sign-in for 12 months are deleted.

entries.q: How do I delete my data or my account?
entries.a: Open the Account page, type DELETE to confirm, and choose "Delete my account and all my data". That cancels anything running, signs you out, and removes your runs, files, results and account within 24 hours. It cannot be undone.

entries.q: Can I import from Google Sheets?
entries.a:
Yes. On the New run or Check my data screen, paste the sheet's link under "Or import from a link" and choose Import.

The sheet must be shared so that anyone with the link can view it (Share, then General access). Any web address that serves a CSV file works too.

entries.q: The Google Sheets import is not working. Why?
alt: google returned a sign in page
entries.a:
Almost always the sheet is private. In Google Sheets choose Share, set General access to "Anyone with the link", then import again.

If the address is not a Google Sheet, the site hosting the file may not allow other websites to fetch it. Download the file and upload it instead.

entries.q: Which data sources can I connect?
alt: does it connect to my ad accounts
entries.a:
Today you can upload a CSV with any column names, import from a Google Sheets or CSV link, add calendar events from the library, and fetch economy figures for the US or UK.

Direct connections to data warehouses such as Snowflake and to ad platforms are not available yet. For now, export a weekly table from them as CSV or to a Google Sheet.

entries.q: What are outside factors, and should I add any?
entries.a:
An outside factor is anything that moves your sales but is not advertising: promotions, price changes, holidays, competitor activity, stock-outs, the wider economy.

Yes, add the ones that matter. They go into the baseline, so advertising is not credited with sales it did not cause. On the real example brands, calendar events alone cut the error on unseen weeks by up to a quarter.

entries.q: How do I add Black Friday or Christmas to the model?
entries.a:
After your data loads, find "Add outside factors from the library". Tick the events that matter (Black Friday week, Cyber week, the run-up to Christmas, Christmas and New Year, Easter) and choose "Add selected to my data".

The dates are worked out from your file. An event that never falls inside your dates is left out, and the screen says which.

entries.q: My business has other key dates. How do I add them?
entries.a:
Add a column to your file that is 1 in the weeks the event applies and 0 in every other week, then mark it as an outside factor (or name it control_<something>).

This works for anything with a date: a product launch, a sale you run each year, Valentine's Day, a local holiday.

entries.q: How do I add economic factors like unemployment or inflation?
entries.a:
Once signed in, load your data and find "The wider economy". Pick the United States or the United Kingdom, tick one or two measures (unemployment, inflation, consumer confidence, interest rate, retail sales growth) and choose "Fetch and add to my data".

Each week gets the previous month's figure, the latest that would have been published at the time. The figures come from FRED, the Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis.

entries.q: Do economic factors actually improve the model?
alt: should i add all economic indicators
entries.a:
Sometimes a lot, often not at all. On the five real brands, unemployment more than halved one brand's error on unseen weeks (25.2% to 11.2%), and consumer confidence with inflation helped another. Nothing helped the other three, and adding every measure at once made four of the five worse.

These series move slowly, so they can stand in for a change in your trend without causing it. Add one or two that plausibly affect your customers, not all of them.

entries.q: Why was an economic measure left out?
entries.a:
A measure is skipped, with the reason shown, when its figures start after your data does, stop more than three months before your data ends, or do not change over your dates.

For example, the UK inflation series currently stops in March 2025, so it is left out for data that runs later.

entries.q: How many outside factors should I add?
alt: can i add too many controls
entries.a:
Few, and only ones with a clear reason to matter. Every factor you add is something else the model must estimate, and factors that drift slowly can soak up the trend or even the effect of advertising.

A good order: events and promotions first, since their timing is sharp and well known; then at most one or two economy or market measures. Check the Baseline drivers chart afterwards: a factor whose range sits across zero is not earning its place.

entries.q: Can I add website traffic or brand search volume as an outside factor?
alt: should i control for web sessions
entries.a:
Be careful. Traffic and searches for your own brand are partly caused by your advertising. Put them in the baseline and they take credit away from the ads that produced them, so advertising looks weaker than it is.

When this was tested on real brands, the brand's own search interest made forecasts worse for two of three and pulled credit from media. Search interest in the product category as a whole is safer, because your ads do not move it much.

entries.q: How do I account for competitors?
entries.a:
If you have a weekly measure, add it as an outside factor: competitor spend estimates, their promotion weeks as a flag, or their share of search.

If you have nothing, the effect ends up in the trend and the noise. A competitor event on a known date is worth flagging even as a simple 1 for the affected weeks.

entries.q: Should I add weather?
entries.a:
Only if your product is plainly weather-driven, such as ice cream, heating or garden furniture. For the five online brands tested, temperature and rain against the seasonal norm helped none of them.

Ordinary seasonal weather is already covered by the yearly seasonal pattern. What can add something is unusual weather, as a difference from normal for that week of the year.

entries.q: Which outside factors helped most in testing?
entries.a:
Scored on weeks the model had not seen, across five real brands:

- Calendar events helped most often, cutting one brand's error from 19.3% to 15.8%.
- Promotion depth helped a little alongside events.
- Unemployment more than halved one brand's error.
- Category search interest gave two brands a small gain.
- Weather helped none. Every economy measure at once made four of five worse.

entries.q: What is a prior?
alt: what is prior knowledge in the model
entries.a:
A prior is what the model assumes about something before it looks at your data. Kawkit's defaults are deliberately weak, so your data leads.

You can replace them with what you actually know. If a test showed TV returns between 0.8 and 2.0, say so, and the model starts from there instead of from scratch.

entries.q: Do I have to fill in the priors? What if I leave them blank?
alt: can i skip the priors step
what to enter for roi range
i have no idea what to enter for the priors
entries.a:
They are all optional. Leave everything blank and the model uses weak defaults and lets your data decide. That is the right choice if you have no solid evidence.

Add a prior only when you have a real reason, such as an experiment. A guess entered as if it were knowledge makes the answer look more certain than it is.

entries.q: What are the default priors?
alt: what does the model assume by default
what priors are used if i leave blank
entries.a:
Every channel starts with the same expected return: the one at which advertising as a whole would explain about 30% of your revenue. The spread around it is wide.

Carry-over starts at about a quarter of a week's effect passing into the next week. Saturation speed has a broad prior. Trend, seasonality and outside factors start centred on no effect.

In addition, the baseline is expected to make up 50% to 90% of revenue, and cannot go below zero in any week.

entries.q: How do I enter an ROI range?
alt: how to fill roi low and high
what is roi low end high end
how do i use a lift test result
entries.a:
On step 2 of a new run, each channel has "ROI, low end" and "ROI, high end". Enter the range you are about 90% sure the true return falls in, for example 0.8 and 2.0.

If a test gave one number with a margin, use the number minus and plus the margin. Add where it came from in the note box; it is kept with the run. Both ends are needed, and low must be above zero.

entries.q: What should I enter for 'effect lasts about (weeks)'?
alt: how many weeks does tv last
what to put in effect lasts
entries.a:
Roughly how many weeks until an ad's effect has almost gone (about 10% left). Leave it blank unless you have a view.

As a guide: search and retargeting act within about a week; social and display over one to three weeks; TV, video and outdoor over three to eight. The model looks back up to eight weeks.

entries.q: It says my ROI ranges are impossible. Why?
alt: roi ranges imply more revenue than i had
entries.a:
Multiply each channel's spend by the low end of the range you gave. If those add up to more than all your revenue, the ranges cannot all be true at once, and the run is blocked.

The usual cause is entering platform-reported ROAS, which counts sales the ads did not cause. Use ranges from experiments, or lower them.

entries.q: What happens if my prior is wrong?
alt: can a prior bias the result
what if i enter a bad prior
entries.a:
If your data is informative, it pulls the answer away from the prior, and the result is flagged: "the data disagrees with your prior". Check where that belief came from.

If your data is not informative for that channel, a wrong prior simply becomes the answer. That is why the Prior vs posterior tab shows both curves: when they look the same, you are reading your own assumption back.

entries.q: How do I run a test to measure a channel properly?
alt: how to run a geo test
entries.a:
The simplest reliable design is a geo test. Pick regions that normally sell alike. Pause or halve the channel in some of them for 4 to 6 weeks and leave the rest alone. The gap in sales between the two groups, divided by the spend you removed, is the channel's return.

Platform lift studies (Meta, Google) do the same with user groups. Enter the result as that channel's ROI range on your next run, and the other channels' estimates sharpen too.

entries.q: Can I re-run a model with different priors?
entries.a:
Yes. Open the run and choose "Re-run with different priors". Your data and earlier entries are loaded for you to change. The new run is separate, so you can use Compare to see how much the answer moved.

If a small change in a prior moves a channel a lot, your data says little about that channel.

entries.q: How long does a run take?
alt: when will my results be ready
entries.a:
Usually a few minutes once it starts. If others are ahead of you, the run page shows your place in the queue and an estimated wait.

You can close the tab. The run carries on, and the result will be under My runs when you come back.

entries.q: Can I close the tab while it runs?
alt: do i need to keep the page open
will it keep running if i close my laptop
entries.a: Yes. Once submitted, the run is fitted on the model server, not in your browser. Close the tab or your laptop and come back later; it will be under My runs.

entries.q: What do the run statuses mean?
entries.a:
- Queued: waiting its turn; the page shows how many are ahead.
- Running: being fitted; a progress bar shows the stage (main fit, then a check on held-out weeks, then summaries).
- Finished: results are ready.
- Failed: something went wrong; the reason is shown.
- Cancelled: you stopped it.

The progress bar is an estimate, not an exact count.

entries.q: How many models can I run at once?
alt: why can't i submit another run
entries.a:
One running and two waiting at a time, and 20 submissions in any 24 hours. If you hit the limit, wait for one to finish or cancel one from My runs.

Your 5 most recent finished runs are kept; older ones are removed when a new one finishes.

entries.q: How do I cancel a run?
entries.a: Open the run and choose "Cancel this run". A waiting run is removed at once. A running one stops within about half a minute. Cancelled runs do not count towards your 5 and are deleted after 7 days.

entries.q: It says the model server is offline. What now?
alt: my run is stuck in the queue
why is my run still queued
entries.a:
The models are fitted on a dedicated machine. When it is offline your run is safe: it waits in the queue and starts by itself when the server is back. You do not need to resubmit.

Past results, the optimiser, the scenario planner and everything else on the site keep working in the meantime.

entries.q: My run failed. What should I do?
entries.a:
Open the run; the reason is shown at the top. The common ones:

- The file did not pass the server's checks: fix what it names and upload again.
- Your ROI ranges are impossible for your data: lower them.
- The server was interrupted three times: submit it again.

Failed runs do not count towards your 5 kept runs.

entries.q: My file was rejected. What do the errors mean?
entries.a:
The message names the problem and the rows, counting the header as row 1. The usual causes:

- a required column is missing, or two columns share a name
- a date that is not a real date, or appears twice
- a cell that is blank or not a number, or negative spend
- rows that are neither 7 days nor 1 day apart
- fewer than 52 weeks

Fix the file and load it again. If only the column names are different, use the column mapper instead.

entries.q: It says a date is not valid. How do I fix it?
entries.a:
Either a date is written in a way that was not recognised, is not a real date (such as 30 February), or is repeated.

If your dates are in another format, the column mapper converts them: pick how they are written under "How dates are written". For a repeated date, add the two rows together or remove the duplicate.

entries.q: It says rows must be 7 days apart. Why?
alt: rows are neither 7 days nor 1 day apart
my weeks start on different days
entries.a:
The model needs regular weeks. Every row must start on the same weekday, 7 days after the last (or every row must be one day, for daily data). The message lists the rows that break the pattern.

Check for a week that starts on a different day, or a stray extra row.

entries.q: How do I sign in or create an account?
entries.a:
Choose Sign in at the top right. Pick "Create account" and enter an email and a password of at least 8 characters, or pick "Email me a link" to sign in without a password.

You stay signed in on that device.

entries.q: How do I read my results? Where do I start?
alt: what should i look at first
i have my results now what
how do i make sense of the results
entries.a:
Start with the "In short" box at the top. It says what to do, how sure the model is, and how far to trust it, in three sentences.

Then check the Convergence check is green. After that the tabs go deeper: Fit (does the model track your sales), Channels (what each one returns), Prior vs posterior (how much your data taught it), Response curves, and Optimise budget.

entries.q: What is the 'In short' box?
alt: what to do how sure how far to trust it
entries.a:
A three-sentence summary written from your result:

- What to do: where to move budget, what that is expected to add, and the chance it beats your current split.
- How sure: which channel returns most, and which very likely do or do not pay back.
- How far to trust it: how well the model predicted weeks it had not seen, and anything to be careful about.

entries.q: What does ROI mean here?
alt: is roi the same as roas
entries.a:
ROI is the revenue a channel brought in divided by what you spent on it, over the whole period. An ROI of 2.5 means every 1 spent returned 2.5 in revenue. Above 1 means it returned more revenue than it cost.

It is the same idea as ROAS. Note it is revenue, not profit: with a 40% margin you need an ROI above 2.5 to make money.

entries.q: What is marginal ROI, and how is it different from ROI?
alt: which roi should i use for budget decisions
entries.a:
ROI is the average return on everything you spent. Marginal ROI is the return on the next unit you would spend, at your recent level.

They differ because of diminishing returns. A channel can have a healthy ROI of 3 overall while the next unit returns only 0.8, because you are already near its limit. For moving budget, marginal ROI is the one that matters: shift money from low marginal ROI to high.

entries.q: What is a 90% range?
alt: what is the bar on the chart
what do low and high mean
entries.a:
It is the range the true value falls in with 90% probability, given the model and your data. On the charts the dot is the median (the best single guess) and the bar is the range.

A narrow bar means your data pinned the value down. A wide bar means several quite different values all fit your data about equally well.

entries.q: What does 'chance it is above 1' mean?
alt: what is the break even line
entries.a:
It is the probability that the channel returned more revenue than it cost. 97% means it almost certainly did; 50% is a coin toss; 5% means it almost certainly did not.

Break-even at 1 is in revenue terms. If your margin is 50%, your real break-even ROI is 2, so read the range against that instead.

entries.q: What do the high, medium and low confidence labels mean?
entries.a:
They compare the width of a channel's ROI range with its middle value. Under half is high confidence, up to the same size is medium, wider than that is low.

Low confidence does not mean the channel is bad. It means your data cannot say much about it yet.

entries.q: Why is the range for one of my channels so wide?
alt: why are my intervals so wide
why is the model so uncertain
how do i narrow the range
why is the bar so long for one channel
entries.a:
Usually one of four reasons: the channel's spend hardly varied; it always moved together with another channel or with the season; it is a small share of spend; or there are few weeks of data.

To narrow it: add more history, vary the spend on purpose, add events so the season is explained separately, or run a test and enter the result as a prior. The "What to test next" box names the channel where that pays off most.

entries.q: What is the convergence check?
entries.a:
It checks the fitting process itself worked. The model is fitted four times independently; if the four agree, the answer is stable.

- R-hat compares the four fits. 1.01 or less is good.
- Effective sample size is how much independent information the fit holds. 400 or more is good.
- Divergent draws are warnings that the fit struggled. Under 0.1% is good.

Green means go ahead. It says the maths ran properly, not that the model is right about your business.

entries.q: My model did not converge. What should I do?
entries.a:
It means the four independent fits disagreed, so the numbers are not stable. On a fail the results are hidden behind a warning; on caution they are shown, but small differences between channels should not be trusted.

It usually happens when the data cannot separate the channels: steady spend, few weeks, many channels, or channels that always move together. Try more history, fewer or merged channels, or priors from experiments.

entries.q: How accurate is the model? How do I read the error figures?
alt: is this level of error acceptable
entries.a:
Each run hides its last 13 weeks, fits again without them, and predicts them. Read three things, in this order:

1. Does it beat a simple forecast? The tile shows the model next to a forecast that needs no model. If it cannot beat that, do not use it to forecast sales.
2. The quarter total. Budgets are set per quarter, and weekly misses that cancel out do not change a decision.
3. The typical week.

On made-up data the weekly miss is about 2%. On real brands 15% to 30% is normal, and a few unusual weeks cause most of it.

entries.q: What is the 'simple forecast' my model is compared with?
alt: model does not beat the simple forecast
entries.a:
The better of two forecasts that need no model at all: the average of the previous 13 weeks, or the same weeks a year earlier scaled for how much you have grown.

If the model cannot beat those, it is not adding forecasting value. It can still be useful for splitting budget between channels, which those simple rules cannot do, and the summary says so when that is the case.

entries.q: What is R² (variation explained)?
entries.a:
It is the share of the week-to-week movement in your sales that the model accounts for, on the data it was fitted to. 100% would be a perfect trace.

High is not proof of a good model: a model can trace past sales closely and still credit the wrong channels. The error on unseen weeks is the harder and more honest test.

entries.q: If the error is low, are the channel estimates right?
alt: does good fit mean correct attribution
can a model predict well and still be wrong
how do i know the roi is right
entries.a:
No. Predicting sales well and splitting the credit correctly are different things. If two channels always move together, the model can forecast perfectly while giving all the credit to the wrong one.

So check more than error: is the fit converged, did your data move the priors, are the ranges narrow, is the baseline believable? The only real proof of a channel's return is an experiment.

entries.q: How can I reduce the error?
alt: client is worried about the error
how do i get the error down
entries.a:
In rough order of what helps most:

1. Add calendar events from the library. Big single weeks cause most of the miss.
2. Add your promotions and price changes as outside factors.
3. Flag one-off weeks such as a stock-out, an outage or a launch.
4. Try one economy measure that plausibly matters to your customers.
5. Add more history.

Then judge it against the simple forecast and on the quarter total, not only the weekly figure.

entries.q: What is the baseline?
alt: what would i sell with no ads
entries.a:
The baseline is what you would have sold with no advertising at all: your brand's standing, repeat customers, the season, and any outside factors you supplied. On the Fit chart it is the dashed line.

Whatever is above the baseline is what the model credits to your paid channels.

entries.q: How big should the baseline be?
alt: what share of sales is baseline
entries.a:
For most established businesses, 50% to 90% of sales would happen without advertising. The model expects the baseline to fall in that range: it has no preference inside it and resists leaving it, though strong evidence in your data can still move it out.

A young, paid-driven brand can genuinely sit lower. But if your baseline comes out well under 50%, the more common cause is that spend follows sales, and the model cannot separate them.

entries.q: The model says most of my revenue comes from advertising. Is that right?
alt: revenue driven by media is very high
model credits too much to ads
it says nearly all my sales come from ads
entries.a:
Probably not, and the summary will warn you when the share is unusually high. It usually means you spend more in the weeks you expect to sell more. The model sees spend and sales rise together and cannot tell which caused which.

What helps: add events and promotions so those weeks are explained; and test your largest channel by holding spend back somewhere. Until then, treat the recommended split as a direction, not a forecast.

entries.q: What is the 'baseline drivers' chart?
entries.a:
It shows what each outside factor you supplied does to weekly revenue, with its range. For an event it is the change in a week when it happens. For a measure such as unemployment it compares its highest observed value with its lowest.

A bar clear of the "no effect" line is a real driver. A bar across the line is not doing much and could be removed.

entries.q: Why does an outside factor show a negative effect?
entries.a:
Often it is real: for many online shops, the week of Christmas and New Year sells less than the weeks before it, so its effect is negative.

For slow-moving measures such as consumer confidence, a surprising direction usually means the measure is tracing your trend, not causing it. It still helps the forecast, but do not read its direction as cause and effect.

entries.q: How do I read the 'Prior vs posterior' tab?
alt: what is the before and after chart
how much did the data move my belief
entries.a:
For each channel there are two curves. The dashed one is the belief before your data (the prior). The solid one is the belief after (the posterior).

A wide dashed curve turning into a narrow solid one means your data was informative. Two curves that look the same mean the result is mostly the assumption you started with. Each channel gets a plain verdict underneath.

entries.q: What do 'the data was decisive' and the other verdicts mean?
entries.a:
They say how far your data moved the starting belief for that channel:

- The data was decisive: the range is more than 50% narrower.
- The data refined the belief: 20% to 50% narrower.
- This mostly reflects the prior: under 20% narrower.
- The data overruled the starting assumption: the result landed outside the range the prior gave.

entries.q: What does 'this mostly reflects the prior' mean?
alt: why did the data not move the prior
entries.a:
Your data told the model almost nothing new about that channel, so the answer is close to what it assumed at the start. It is the honest result when a channel's spend barely varied, was tiny, or always moved with something else.

Do not base a decision on that number. Vary the spend, or test the channel.

entries.q: What is carry-over (adstock)?
alt: do ads keep working after they run
entries.a:
Advertising keeps working after it runs. Someone sees a TV ad this week and buys in three weeks' time. Carry-over is how the model spreads a week's spend over the weeks that follow.

Each channel gets its own rate, learned from your data, looking back up to eight weeks. Without it, slow channels would be badly undervalued.

entries.q: What is the carry-over half-life?
alt: how long does the effect last chart
entries.a: The number of weeks until half of a week's advertising effect has played out. A half-life of 0.5 means it works almost at once, typical for search. Two or more weeks means a slow build and a long tail, typical for TV and video.

entries.q: What are diminishing returns (saturation)?
alt: why does more spend return less
entries.a:
Each extra unit you spend on a channel adds a little less than the one before. The first 1,000 reaches your keenest customers; the next 1,000 reaches people less likely to buy. Eventually more spend adds almost nothing.

The model learns this curve for each channel. It is why "put everything into the best channel" is rarely right.

entries.q: How do I read a response curve?
alt: what is the response curve chart
what do the dashed lines on the curve mean
entries.a:
It shows the weekly revenue a channel is expected to bring in at each level of steady weekly spend, with a shaded range.

Where the curve is steep, more spend still pays. Where it flattens, you are near saturation. One marker shows where you spend now; another shows the highest week in your data. To the right of that second marker the model has never seen the channel, so it is guessing.

entries.q: What is contribution?
alt: how much revenue did each channel drive
entries.a:
The revenue the model credits to a channel. "Total contribution" adds it up over the whole period; "contribution over time" shows it week by week, including the weeks after the spend when carry-over is still working.

Contribution divided by spend is the ROI.

entries.q: Why is my ROI here lower than what Facebook or Google report?
alt: meta says roas 6 but kawkit says 2
why don't the numbers match ads manager
entries.a:
Ad platforms count every sale that touched one of their ads, including people who would have bought anyway, and several platforms often claim the same sale. So their figures add up to more than you actually sold.

This model only credits a channel with sales that moved when its spend moved. That is closer to the truth of what the spend caused, and it is nearly always lower.

entries.q: What is incrementality?
alt: would those sales have happened anyway
entries.a:
Incremental sales are the ones that happened because of the advertising and would not have happened without it. That is the only kind worth paying for.

A model of past data estimates it by comparing weeks. An experiment measures it directly, by switching the advertising off for some people or places and seeing what is lost. The model is the map; experiments are the survey points that keep it honest.

entries.q: The tool works in revenue. How do I think about profit?
entries.a:
Divide 1 by your margin to get your real break-even ROI. At a 40% margin it is 2.5; at 25% it is 4. Read each channel's range against that line, not against 1.

Or model profit directly: put weekly gross profit in the revenue column, and ROI above 1 then does mean profitable. The recommended split is the same either way if your margin is the same across channels.

entries.q: How does the budget optimiser work?
alt: how is the recommended split worked out
how does it decide where to move money
entries.a:
It looks for the weekly spend per channel that gives the most expected revenue for your budget, within limits you set. It moves money from channels where the next unit returns little to channels where it returns more, until no move helps.

It does this across 500 versions of the model that all fit your data, which is how it can say how likely the new split is to beat your current one. It runs in your browser, so changing a number updates the answer at once.

entries.q: What does 'chance the new split beats your current one' mean?
entries.a:
The model is not one answer but 500 that all fit your data. The recommended split is tried under each. If it earns more than your current split in 470 of them, the chance is 94%.

Above about 90% is a strong signal. Near 50% means the limits or budget leave little room, or the model is too unsure to call it.

entries.q: How much more revenue will the recommended split bring?
entries.a:
The Recommendation panel shows the expected change in weekly revenue from media, with a 90% range. If the range is all above zero, the gain is very likely real. If it straddles zero, it may be nothing.

It assumes you hold the new spend steady and that the future behaves like the past. Treat it as a direction and a rough size, and move in steps.

entries.q: How do I set limits or lock a channel in the optimiser?
alt: i can't cut tv below a contract
entries.a:
In "Budget and limits", set the weekly budget and a minimum and maximum for each channel, or tick Lock to keep a channel at its current spend. Limits start at 50% to 150% of what you spend now, and the budget starts at your average over the last 13 weeks.

Use limits for real constraints: a contract minimum, or a cap on how fast you are willing to move. "Reset to defaults" undoes your changes.

entries.q: It says the budget is below the minimums (or above the maximums). Why?
alt: budget is below the sum of the channel minimums
entries.a:
Your budget and limits cannot both be met. If the channel minimums already add up to more than the budget, the plan uses the minimums and tells you. The same happens in reverse when the maximums add up to less than the budget.

Change the budget, or loosen a limit.

entries.q: What does 'beyond your data' mean?
alt: spend more than the highest week
entries.a:
The plan would spend more on a channel than 1.2 times the highest week in your data. The model has never seen that channel at that level, so it is stretching its curve past the evidence.

It may still be right, but treat that part with caution and scale up in steps while you watch the result.

entries.q: Can I try my own budget split?
alt: what if i cut tv by half
what happens if i spend more
entries.a:
Yes. On the Optimise budget tab, under "Try your own split", type any weekly spend per channel. You see the expected change in revenue with its range, the chance it beats what you do now, and what each extra unit returns.

There are quick buttons to cut or raise everything by 20%. Nothing is refitted, so it answers instantly.

entries.q: How much budget do I need to hit a revenue target?
alt: how do i reach my revenue goal
i need more revenue how much should i spend
entries.a:
On the Optimise budget tab, under "Work back from a target", enter the extra weekly revenue you want. It finds the smallest budget the model expects to deliver it, the split to use, and the chance of getting there.

Each channel may go from half to twice its current spend. If the target cannot be reached within that, it says so and gives the most that is possible, because returns flatten as spend grows.

entries.q: What is 'What to test next'?
alt: where should i run an experiment
which channel should i experiment on
entries.a:
At the top of the Channels tab, it names the channel where an experiment would be worth most: the one where a lot of money rides on a very uncertain return. It shows the weekly revenue at stake for each channel.

Testing a small channel, or one the model is already sure about, teaches you little. This points you at the one that would change your decisions.

entries.q: How should I act on the recommendation?
alt: should i follow the recommended split
how to use the results in practice
what do i do with this
should i move all my budget
how fast should i change spend
entries.a:
Move in steps, not all at once. A sensible pattern:

1. Shift 10% to 20% of the way towards the recommended split.
2. Hold it for 4 to 8 weeks.
3. Add the new weeks to your data and run again.

Act most boldly where the chance of improvement is high and the channel is well measured. Where a channel is marked low confidence or "mostly reflects the prior", test it before betting on it.

entries.q: The model says a channel has ROI below 1. Should I switch it off?
alt: should i stop a channel with low roi
entries.a:
Not straight away. First check how sure the model is: a low middle value with a wide range, or one that mostly reflects the prior, is not evidence. Check too whether break-even at 1 is the right line for your margin.

If it is well measured and clearly below your break-even, cut it in steps and watch total sales. Some channels look poor on their own but support others, such as video building demand that search then collects.

entries.q: How often should I re-run the model?
alt: when should i refresh the model
entries.a:
Every quarter is a good rhythm, and after any big change: a new channel, a large shift in budget, or a test result. Add the new weeks to your file and submit again.

Running weekly adds little, since one more week barely changes two years of history. Use Compare to see what moved between runs.

entries.q: What exactly is the model?
entries.a:
Weekly revenue is modelled as a baseline plus each channel's contribution, with normal noise.

- Baseline: intercept, linear trend, two yearly sine and cosine pairs (with 78 weeks or more), and your outside factors.
- Each channel: spend is scaled, passed through normalised geometric adstock over 8 weeks, then a logistic saturation curve, and multiplied by a non-negative effect.

It is written in PyMC and sampled with NUTS (nutpie): 4 chains of 1,000 draws after 1,000 warm-up steps, and each run stores its random seed so it can be reproduced exactly.

entries.q: How does the model handle seasonality and trend?
entries.a:
It fits a straight-line trend and a smooth yearly pattern, so regular highs and lows through the year go into the baseline, not to advertising. The yearly pattern is only used when you have 78 weeks or more.

A smooth curve cannot follow a single huge week such as Black Friday. Add those from the event library.

entries.q: My growth rate changed part-way through. Can the model handle that?
entries.a:
Only partly. The trend is one straight line. A trend that can change pace each quarter was tested and made forecasts worse on all five real brands, because it carries its latest pace forward and overshoots, so it was not adopted.

If there was a clear break, such as a relaunch or a new market, add an outside factor that is 0 before it and 1 after. Or use only the data since the break, if that still leaves a year or more.

entries.q: Two of my channels always move together. Is that a problem?
alt: channels spend in the same weeks
entries.a:
Yes. If two channels always rise and fall in the same weeks, the model sees their combined effect but cannot say how to divide it. Typically both get wide ranges, or one gets the credit somewhat arbitrarily.

Either merge them into one channel, since you cannot learn them apart anyway, or stagger their spend for a while, or test one of them.

entries.q: We spend more when we expect to sell more. Does that bias the result?
alt: budget set as a percent of revenue
we scale spend in peak season
entries.a:
Yes, and it is the commonest way these models mislead. If budgets follow expected demand, spend and sales rise together for reasons that have nothing to do with the ads working, and the model credits the advertising.

It cannot be fully fixed from past data. It is reduced by explaining demand separately (events, promotions, seasonality) and by the expectation that most sales are baseline. It is only removed by spending against the pattern on purpose, which is what a test does.

entries.q: How should I treat branded search?
alt: brand search roi looks too high
should brand keywords be a channel
entries.a:
Keep it apart from generic search, and read its result sceptically. People searching for your name were mostly coming anyway; the ad often just takes the click that the free result below it would have got.

Because branded search rises whenever demand rises, a model of past data tends to flatter it. A simple test settles it: switch it off for two weeks in one region and see whether total sales fall.

entries.q: Does the model capture channels helping each other?
entries.a:
No. Each channel's effect is added independently. If TV makes people search for you, the sale tends to be credited to whichever of the two varied most clearly, usually search.

So be cautious about cutting an awareness channel just because its own return looks modest. Test it by cutting it somewhere and watching total sales, including the channels it may be feeding.

entries.q: Does this measure long-term brand building?
entries.a:
No. It measures what advertising does within about eight weeks. Slower effects, such as a stronger brand that lifts sales for years, show up in the baseline and are not credited to the campaigns that built it.

That means brand and awareness channels are undervalued here. Use this for the short-term picture, and judge long-term brand spend with brand tracking and longer tests.

entries.q: I just started a new channel. Can it be modelled?
alt: channel with only a few weeks of data
entries.a:
Include it, so its sales are not given to another channel, but expect a wide range until it has run for a few months with some variation. A channel active in under 15% of your weeks gets a warning.

If you have a benchmark or a platform lift study for it, enter that as a prior.

entries.q: Does a channel's effectiveness change over time in the model?
entries.a:
No. Each channel has one return for the whole period, which is an average. If a channel has clearly changed, for example after a tracking change or a new creative approach, the average blends before and after.

A practical workaround is to model only the recent period, if that leaves at least a year, or to run two periods separately and compare them.

entries.q: Is my business too small for this?
alt: does mmm work for small brands
entries.a:
Size matters less than variation. What the model needs is channels that are each a meaningful share of spend and that go up and down over two years or so.

Very low weekly sales are a real limit, though. With a few dozen orders a week, chance alone moves sales by 15% to 20%, and no model can see through that. In that case model a steadier outcome, or use the tool for the direction of budget, not to forecast.

entries.q: How does this compare with Robyn, Meridian or PyMC-Marketing?
entries.a:
Those are code libraries for data scientists; Kawkit is a no-code service built on the same family of methods. It uses the geometric adstock and logistic saturation found in PyMC-Marketing, in a Bayesian model like Meridian's. Robyn takes a non-Bayesian route.

The libraries offer more: several regions in one model, effects that change over time, reach and frequency. Kawkit trades that for minutes instead of days, and for plain-language output.

entries.q: Will I get the same answer if I run the same data twice?
alt: why are two runs slightly different
entries.a:
Each run has its own random seed, so two separate submissions of the same file give slightly different numbers, within the ranges shown. That is expected with this kind of fitting.

If two runs of the same data differ a lot, the model is not well pinned down by your data: check the convergence check and how wide the ranges are.

entries.q: How do I share a result with someone?
alt: how long does a share link last
entries.a:
Open a finished run and choose Share. You get a link that anyone can open without an account, for 30 days. Choose "Stop sharing" to switch it off at once.

People with the link see the results only. They cannot see your uploaded file, your other runs or your account, and they get the stored recommendation without the interactive optimiser.

entries.q: Can I download my results?
entries.a:
Yes, from the Download tab, as CSV files: channel results, weekly fit and contributions, the recommended split, and a posterior summary. The Optimise budget tab also downloads the split for whatever budget and limits you have set.

Every chart has a "Show table" button too.

entries.q: Can I get a PDF report?
entries.a: Yes. Choose "Open printable report" above the results. It puts every section on one page, with the recommended split. Then choose "Print or save as PDF" and pick Save as PDF in your browser's print window.

entries.q: How do I compare two runs?
entries.a:
When you have two finished runs, My runs shows "Compare two runs". Pick run A and run B to see each channel's ROI range side by side, plus fit and convergence for both.

It is the quickest way to see what a new prior, new weeks of data or a different channel grouping changed.

entries.q: Can I rename a run?
alt: change the name of a run
entries.a: Yes. Open the run and choose Rename.

entries.q: Does it work on a phone?
alt: can i use it on my phone
entries.a: Yes, down to a small phone screen, in current versions of Chrome, Edge, Firefox and Safari. Charts are easier to read on a larger screen, and every chart has a table view.

entries.q: Who are you?
entries.a:
I'm Neon, Kawkit's guide. I answer from a fixed set of questions and answers about the tool and about marketing mix modelling, written by the people who built it.

I am not a live AI and I cannot see your data or your results, so I can explain what a number means but not tell you what yours is. Ask in your own words, or pick a topic below.

entries.q: What can I ask you?
entries.a:
I can help with:

- Getting started and what the tool does
- Preparing your data and connecting sources
- Adding what you already know (priors)
- Running a model and what the statuses mean
- Reading results: ROI, ranges, accuracy, baseline
- Budget planning: optimiser, scenarios, targets, what to test
- How the model works, for the technically minded

entries.q: Hello
entries.a: Hello, I'm Neon. Ask me anything about Kawkit or about marketing mix modelling, from "what is this?" to "why is my baseline so low?".

entries.q: Thank you
entries.a: You're welcome. Ask me anything else whenever you like.

entries.q: Goodbye
entries.a: Goodbye, and good luck with the budget.

entries.q: How do I contact support or report a problem?
entries.a:
I can only answer from my prepared answers, and there is no live support chat. If something looks broken, note what you did and what you saw, and send it to whoever shared Kawkit with you.

If a run failed, the reason is shown on its page, and I can explain most of them.
